segments: The Chronography of Barhebraeus.
68. [reigned] seven years.
And in that same year, Bahram reigned in Persia for three years.
And after him, Bahram his son, seventeen years.
And Sotranilus (Saturninus?) the prefect,
when he sought to rebel and make himself king over the Romans,
began to build Antioch,
and he was killed in Apamea.
And Probus Caesar was also killed in Sirmium, [having reigned] years {OCR?}
after Probus, two.
And when Carus died in Mesopotamia of Syria,
his son Numerian was also killed in the region of Africa.
Carinus, however, his other son, was likewise killed by chance in the war against the Germans.
twenty {OCR?} years.
And {OCR?} three others also reigned with him:
Maximian, who gave his daughter to Diocletian,
and was called Herculius;
and both of them jointly administered in the East.
And Maxentius, the son of Maximian, who governed in Rome.
And Constantius (Constantius?) in Gaul and in Britain.
And from the first year of Diocletian, which is the year five hundred and ninety-five of the Greeks (284 of our Lord?);
and the year five thousand seven hundred and seventy-five from Adam;
and from here begins the era of the Egyptians.
And at that time Egypt rebelled,
and the Romans went and subjugated it,
and they slaughtered {OCR?} many.
And in the eleventh year of Diocletian, Narseh reigned in Persia for seven years.
And after him, his son Hormizd, five years.
And in the nineteenth year of Diocletian,
as the great feast of Pascha drew near,
he commanded that the churches of the Christians be demolished to the foundations,
and that the books be burned with fire,
and that whoever would not sacrifice should die.
And many chosen and valiant martyrs were perfected:
George and Bacchus;
and he cut off the tongue of Romanus.
And in his days Nicolaus the martyr was judged, and Azazael of Samosata {OCR?}, the illustrious martyr.
Now that Diocletian, when he was stricken by the Lord,
and his palate {OCR?} was wasted away,
perceived that it was a plague from God;
therefore he wrote to every place
that the Christians should openly conduct themselves according to their customs,
and should rebuild their churches.
